title: Physical Geography — Earth's Systems
description: Study Earth as a system of interacting spheres.
objectives: Identify the four spheres: lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere

lessons.title: Earth's Four Spheres
lessons.content: Earth's systems are divided into four interacting spheres.
examples: Lithosphere: solid rock of Earth's crust
Hydrosphere: all water on, above, and below Earth's surface
Atmosphere: gases surrounding Earth
Biosphere: all living organisms and their environments

lessons.title: Sphere Interactions
lessons.content: Events in one sphere trigger changes in others.
examples: Volcanic eruption (lithosphere) → ash in atmosphere → reduced sunlight → cooler temperatures → impact on biosphere
Deforestation (biosphere) → less evapotranspiration → changed rainfall → drier lithosphere
Ocean warming (hydrosphere) → more evaporation → stronger hurricanes (atmosphere)

title: Human Geography — Migration Patterns
description: Analyze historical and contemporary migration patterns and their causes.

lessons.title: Types of Migration
lessons.content: Migration takes many forms driven by different factors.
examples: Voluntary migration: moving for economic opportunity or better quality of life
Forced migration: fleeing war, persecution, or natural disaster
Internal migration: moving within a country (Great Migration of Black Americans northward)
International migration: crossing national borders

lessons.title: Contemporary Migration
examples: ~280 million international migrants today (~3.5% of world population)
Remittances: migrants send ~$800 billion annually to home countries — more than total foreign aid
Climate migration: rising seas and drought are creating new migration pressures

title: Economic Geography — Development
description: Understand the geography of economic development and inequality.
objectives: Explain geographic factors that influence development

lessons.title: Measuring Development
lessons.content: Development is measured by multiple indicators beyond just income.
examples: GDP per capita: income per person
Human Development Index (HDI): combines income, education (years of schooling), and health (life expectancy)
Top HDI countries: Norway, Switzerland, Iceland; lowest: Niger, South Sudan, Chad

lessons.title: Geography and Development
lessons.content: Geography doesn't determine destiny, but it creates advantages and disadvantages.
examples: Landlocked countries face higher trade costs (no sea access)
Tropical disease burden: malaria costs Africa ~$12 billion/year in lost productivity
Resource curse: oil-rich nations often have weak institutions

title: Political Geography — Borders and Power
description: Analyze political geography and how power shapes spaces.
objectives: Understand how borders are created and contested
Describe international organizations and their geographic dimensions

lessons.title: Sovereignty and Borders
lessons.content: Sovereignty is the right of a state to govern its territory without external interference.
examples: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia established the modern concept of national sovereignty
International law recognizes states' right to their territory
Disputed territories: Kashmir, Gaza, Taiwan, South China Sea — sovereignty contested

title: Environmental Geography — Climate and Society
description: Analyze the geography of climate vulnerability and resilience.
objectives: Explain how poverty amplifies climate risk
Evaluate adaptation strategies in different geographic contexts

lessons.title: Climate Vulnerability
lessons.content: Climate change affects all regions, but some are far more vulnerable than others.
examples: Small Island Developing States (SIDS): Kiribati, Tuvalu, Maldives — existential threat from sea level rise
Sub-Saharan Africa: already faces extreme heat, drought, and flooding
Arctic: warming at 3× the global average; permafrost thaw releasing methane

lessons.title: Adaptation Strategies
lessons.content: Countries and communities are adapting to climate change in various ways.
examples: Netherlands: building floating homes and expanding flood defenses
Bangladesh: constructing floating schools; planting mangroves as natural barriers
Kiribati: purchasing land in Fiji to relocate population if needed

title: Regional Geography — Central and South Asia
description: Study the geography, cultures, and geopolitics of Central and South Asia.
objectives: Explain the strategic importance of Central Asia

lessons.title: Central Asia
lessons.content: Central Asia occupies a strategic crossroads between Europe, Middle East, and East Asia.
examples: Five 'Stans': Kazakhstan (largest), Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan — all former Soviet republics
Enormous oil and gas reserves: Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan
The Aral Sea disaster: one of the worst environmental disasters in history

lessons.title: South Asia
lessons.content: South Asia is home to ~1.9 billion people — nearly a quarter of humanity.
examples: India: 1.4 billion people; world's largest democracy; fastest-growing major economy
Pakistan: 220 million; nuclear power; geographic challenges: flooding, water scarcity
Bangladesh: world's most densely populated large country; 1,080 people/km²
Himalaya: source of 10 rivers serving ~2 billion people

title: Urban Geography — Cities of the Future
description: Analyze urbanization trends and the design of future cities.

lessons.title: Global Urbanization
lessons.content: For the first time in history, more than half the world's population lives in cities.
examples: In 1800: ~3% of people lived in cities; today: ~56%; by 2050: ~68%
Most growth is in developing world: Lagos, Kinshasa, Dhaka, Mumbai
Megacities: 10 million+; there are 35 today; 48 projected by 2035

lessons.title: Smart Cities
lessons.content: Technology is transforming how cities are planned and managed.
examples: Singapore: uses sensors and data to optimize traffic, energy use, and waste
Songdo (South Korea): purpose-built smart city with underground waste collection and real-time monitoring
Barcelona: smart street lighting, smart parking, free public Wi-Fi citywide

title: Water Geography — Global Water Crisis
description: Analyze the geography of freshwater availability and the global water crisis.
objectives: Map the global distribution of fresh water
Evaluate solutions to the water crisis

lessons.title: Water Distribution
lessons.content: Fresh water is unevenly distributed and increasingly scarce.
examples: Only 0.3% of all water is accessible fresh water (rivers, lakes, groundwater)
Water stress: a region uses more than 40% of available water supply
Most water-stressed: Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia, parts of India and China

lessons.title: Solutions
lessons.content: Technological and policy solutions exist but require investment and cooperation.
examples: Desalination: removing salt from seawater — effective but energy-intensive (Israel gets 70% of drinking water this way)
Drip irrigation: delivers water directly to roots; 30-50% more efficient than sprinkler systems
Virtual water trade: countries import water-intensive goods rather than growing them
The Indus Waters Treaty (1960): India-Pakistan water-sharing agreement — held through wars

title: Food Geography — Feeding the World
description: Analyze the geography of food production, distribution, and food security.
objectives: Evaluate sustainability of global food systems

lessons.title: Global Food Production
lessons.content: Food production is geographically concentrated but unevenly distributed.
examples: The U.S., Brazil, China, India, and EU produce most of the world's food
Major grains: wheat (northern plains, Europe, China), rice (Asia), corn (Americas, Africa)
Just 5 crops (wheat, rice, corn, potatoes, soybeans) provide 60% of human calories

lessons.title: Food Insecurity
lessons.content: 815 million people are chronically hungry; 3 billion cannot afford a healthy diet.
examples: Most hunger is in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
Food deserts in wealthy countries: urban areas without access to affordable fresh food
Climate change is reducing crop yields in vulnerable regions

title: Geospatial Technology and the Future of Geography
description: Explore cutting-edge geographic technologies shaping the future.
objectives: Explain remote sensing and its applications
Describe real-world uses of GIS and geospatial big data
Evaluate geographic dimensions of artificial intelligence

lessons.title: Remote Sensing and Big Data
lessons.content: Satellites and sensors generate vast geographic data that transforms decision-making.
examples: Landsat (NASA): 50+ years of Earth imagery; tracks deforestation, glacier loss, urban growth
Planet Labs: daily satellite images of every point on Earth
Google Maps: uses GPS, crowdsourced data, satellite imagery, and street-level photography

lessons.title: Geography and AI
lessons.content: Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing geographic analysis.
examples: Machine learning: analyzes satellite images to count trees, identify land use, or detect illegal mining
Predictive models: forecast disease outbreaks, flood risk, or conflict based on geographic patterns
Autonomous vehicles rely on extremely precise geographic data
The geographic digital divide: benefits flow mainly to wealthy, connected countries
